title: Digital Exams Are a Solution in Search of a Problem
author: David Didau
summary: The push for universal digital exams in UK schools proceeds with boosterism outrunning evidence. AQA's chief executive claims there is 'almost no downside,' but David Didau argues that higher scores on typed exams don't necessarily mean better assessment—they may reflect mode effects rather than improved demonstration of knowledge. The central validity problem is construct-irrelevant variance: if keyboard fluency affects a history grade when it isn't part of the history construct, the exam is measuring something it claims not to. Independent research from Cambridge (2024) and Ofqual (2025) found no clear or consistent performance pattern when comparing digital and paper exams, with results varying by subject, task, and student. Universal digital exams would also create new inequalities, since schools with better device access produce students with medium familiarity advantages. Students who genuinely struggle with handwriting can already apply for access arrangements permitting keyboard use—that specific problem doesn't require overhauling all examinations.
points: Higher typed scores don't confirm assessment improvement—the phrase 'better answers' conceals whether improvement reflects real knowledge or simply familiarity with the medium.
Construct-irrelevant variance is the central validity problem: if keyboard speed affects a history grade, the exam measures something outside its intended construct.
Universal digital exams would expose existing technology access inequalities to high-stakes assessment rather than reduce them—well-resourced schools start with a medium-familiarity advantage.
The argument for teaching digital fluency doesn't entail that GCSE grades should depend on keyboard speed, just as the value of first aid doesn't make it a hidden component of every subject exam.
Students who genuinely struggle with handwriting can already apply for access arrangements permitting keyboard use; that specific problem doesn't require overhauling all examinations.
quotes: Young people are often described as digital natives, yet familiarity with social media tells us very little about whether they can type efficiently, manage files, use spreadsheets, navigate complex software or work productively on screen.
The central question shouldn’t be whether digital exams are possible or popular but whether they allow us to make more valid, reliable and fair judgements about what students know and can do.
One difficulty is that higher scores don’t, by themselves, tell us that an assessment has improved.
An assessment shouldn’t reward the physical ease with which a student can form letters when handwriting is irrelevant to the subject being assessed.
Digital fluency ought to involve judgement, adaptation, verification and purposeful use. Keyboard speed is narrower and more contingent.
Assessment creates incentives which inevitably backwash into the curriculum.
